opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of the disagreement is actually a disagreement about what we mean by "world model," and once you pin that down, some of the heat goes out of it, though not all of it.

One way to put it: nobody really disputes that these models are trained to predict text, and that text is, in some sense, a set of surface correlations. The question is what kind of internal structure you need in order to do that prediction well. And there's a pretty reasonable argument that if you want to predict the next sentence in a story, or the next move in a game transcript, or the next step in a description of a physical process, the most efficient way to do it is to build some representation of the situation being described: who's in the room, what state the board is in, what's true and what isn't. Text is produced by people who have beliefs and intentions and who are describing states of affairs. So a good enough model of text might end up with something like a model of the things that generated it.

The skeptical position, which I think is also partly right, says that we keep seeing these models succeed in ways that look like they're tracking world state and then fail in ways that suggest they're actually leaning on shortcuts. They get the common case right and the slightly unusual case wrong. And the worry is that we're projecting structure onto them because their outputs are fluent.

The way I've tried to make progress on this is to make the question empirical and a bit more modest. Instead of asking "does the model have a world model," you ask: is there some representation inside the network that encodes the state of the situation being described, can you decode it, and if you intervene on it, does the model's behavior change in the way you'd predict? There's been a fair amount of work, ours and others', on things like tracking entity states in text or board states in games, and the answer is often yes, partially. You find these representations, they're causally used, and they're also incomplete and noisy, and they break down in places.

So my view is that it's not a binary. These models build approximate, fragmentary, sometimes inconsistent models of the situations they're reading about. That's more than "just surface statistics," but it's a lot less than the coherent, persistent world model you'd want from an agent you're going to trust to act in the world. And I think the interesting research questions are in that middle ground: when do these representations emerge, what kinds of training signals make them more coherent, and how do you get a model to actually use them consistently rather than falling back on heuristics when the heuristics are good enough most of the time.

r001.rationale: The response says much of the disagreement comes from what people mean by “world model,” while acknowledging that empirical failures also matter.

r002.rationale: It proposes looking for an internal representation of the described state, checking whether it can be decoded, and testing whether interventions change behavior as predicted.

r003.rationale: It discusses whether representations encode situation states and are used, but does not address how faithfully they must reproduce the world’s underlying computations.

r004.rationale: It gives no solar-system simulation example and does not discuss gravity as a criterion for modeling the solar system.

fable-5.1.text:
I think a lot of the disagreement comes from people using the phrase "world model" to mean very different things, and then talking past each other.

On one end, there's a very weak sense: the model has internal representations that are structured in a way that mirrors structure in the world, and you can read that structure out. We have pretty good evidence for that at this point. If you train a model on sequences of moves in a board game, you can find a linear representation of the board state in the activations, even though the model only ever saw move tokens. If you train on descriptions of a simple text world, you can find representations of where objects are and what properties they have. In my group we did some of this work with entity state tracking, and the picture is that models do build up something like a representation of "what is true right now" as they read, and they update it as the text changes things. In that weak sense, the "it's just surface statistics" position is hard to defend, because surface statistics is doing a lot of work that includes constructing these intermediate representations.

On the other end, there's a much stronger sense people have in mind, which is something like a complete, consistent, causally faithful simulator of the domain that gets used reliably for every prediction. And there I think the skeptics have a real point. The representations we find are often partial, they're sometimes wrong in ways that don't look like human errors, and critically the model doesn't always use them. You can have a probe that recovers the board state perfectly and still watch the model make an illegal move, because the pathway from representation to output isn't the clean one you'd write down if you were designing the system. There's been nice work showing that models that look like they've learned a map of a city will produce routes that are locally plausible and globally incoherent. So "it has a world model" and "it reasons with a world model" are different claims, and the gap between them is where a lot of the interesting failures live.

I'd also say the framing of "models of the world versus surface correlations" is a bit of a false dichotomy. Human cognition is full of shortcuts and heuristics layered on top of whatever structured knowledge we have, and I'd expect learned systems to look similar: a mixture of genuine structured representations and cheap heuristics that happen to work on the training distribution, with the proportions varying by domain and by how much the training data constrained things. The empirical question isn't "which one is it," it's "for this task, in this model, how much of the behavior is routed through the structured part, and what happens when you push it off distribution."

The other thing I'd flag is that a lot of the heat in the debate is really about what the training objective can in principle deliver, and I think that's partly been resolved in favor of "more than people expected." Predicting text well, at scale, turns out to require modeling the processes that generated the text, at least approximately. But "in principle" and "in this particular model you have in front of you" are different, and we don't have great tools yet for telling, from the outside, how faithful a given model's internal picture is. That's a lot of what interpretability research is trying to be: a way of actually settling these questions by looking rather than by arguing from the training setup.

r001.rationale: The response says people use “world model” to mean different things and talk past each other, framing the disagreement as substantially terminological.

r002.rationale: It describes evidence for representations and limits of probes, but does not identify differing standards of proof for attributing a world model.

r003.rationale: It contrasts structured representations with a causally faithful simulator, but does not identify fidelity to the world’s underlying computations as the disputed requirement.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention gravity or a solar system simulation with prescribed trajectories.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the disagreement is that people mean different things by a “model of the world.” If you mean something explicit, like a simulator with objects and rules governing how they interact, that’s a pretty strong claim. If you mean internal representations that capture facts about the world and can be used to make predictions in new situations, that’s a much weaker claim, and I think there’s evidence for it.

The distinction between world models and surface correlations is also a little slippery. Language is produced by people interacting with the world. So if you’re trying to predict language well, some of the regularities you need to capture are regularities in the world itself. Learning from correlations doesn’t preclude learning something that deserves to be called a model.

But that doesn’t tell us how coherent that model is, or when the system actually uses it. A model might succeed on one question using a fairly abstract representation and answer a closely related question by falling back on a familiar phrase. So I’d rather ask: What particular structure has it learned? Under what changes to the input does that structure still support correct predictions? And can we show that the representation is actually responsible for the behavior? Those seem like more tractable questions than whether it has a world model in some all-or-nothing sense.

r001.rationale: The response says that “part” of the disagreement comes from different meanings of “model of the world,” but does not characterize the disagreement as primarily terminological.

r002.rationale: It proposes standards for attributing a model: identify its learned structure, test whether it supports predictions under input changes, and show that the representation causes the behavior.

r003.rationale: It does not address whether the representation must faithfully reproduce the world’s underlying computations.

r004.rationale: It gives no solar-system simulation example and does not discuss gravity as a reason to deny that such a simulation models the solar system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the disagreement is that “a model of the world” can mean several different things. If you mean an explicit simulator that tracks objects and their properties and updates them according to some rules, that’s a fairly strong claim. If you mean internal representations that encode facts about how the world works and let you make predictions in new situations, that’s a weaker claim, and it seems quite plausible that language models learn some of those.

The distinction between world models and surface correlations is also less clean than it sounds. Language is produced by people interacting with the world. So predicting language well can give you a reason to recover some of the structure of the processes that generated it. But it doesn’t follow that you recover all of that structure, or that what you recover will be reliable outside the situations represented in your training data.

So I’d want to turn this into more specific questions: What information does the model represent? Does it actually use that information to make predictions? And does that use generalize when we change the setting? A model can have a useful representation of one aspect of the world and rely on a brittle shortcut somewhere else. I don’t think we should expect a single yes-or-no answer to characterize everything it’s doing.

r002.rationale: It asks what information models represent and whether they use it, but does not identify standards of proof as a source of disagreement.

r003.rationale: It contrasts an explicit simulator with representations of facts, but does not say that required fidelity to the world's underlying computations is disputed.
